title: Level 5: Timers — Timer0 Normal Mode & Overflow Interrupt
aim: To use the ATmega328P's Timer/Counter 0 hardware module in Normal Mode, configuring the Timer Overflow Interrupt to blink an LED at a precise 1-second interval without blocking the main program with software delay loops.
objective: Master the Timer0 register set (TCNT0, TCCR0B, TIMSK0), understand the relationship between CPU clock, prescaler, and overflow period, configure ISR(TIMER0_OVF_vect), and implement non-blocking timing using an overflow counter.
theory:
Why Hardware Timers?

Software delay loops (_delay_ms()) are blocking — the CPU does nothing else while waiting. For real embedded systems that must simultaneously read sensors, communicate over UART, and control outputs, this is unacceptable. The ATmega328P contains dedicated hardware timer/counter peripherals that count independently of the CPU, firing an interrupt when they reach configured thresholds — leaving the CPU 100% free for other work.

Timer/Counter 0 — Architecture

Timer0 is an 8-bit timer, meaning its counter register TCNT0 counts from 0 up to 255 (0xFF). On the next tick after 255, it overflows back to 0 and hardware sets the TOV0 (Timer Overflow Flag) bit in TIFR0. In Normal Mode, this overflow cycle repeats endlessly. The timer is driven by the system clock through a configurable prescaler.

The Prescaler — Slowing Down the Clock

At 16 MHz, a raw tick occurs every 62.5 nanoseconds. Without a prescaler, TCNT0 would overflow every 256 × 62.5 ns = 16 µs — too fast for most applications. A prescaler divides the system clock before feeding it to the timer. The available prescaler values and their effects at 16 MHz:

  • ÷1: Tick = 62.5 ns, Overflow = 16 µs
  • ÷8: Tick = 0.5 µs, Overflow = 128 µs
  • ÷64: Tick = 4 µs, Overflow = 1.024 ms
  • ÷256: Tick = 16 µs, Overflow = 4.096 ms
  • ÷1024: Tick = 64 µs, Overflow = 16.384 ms

With prescaler ÷1024, one overflow takes ≈ 16.38 ms. To achieve a 1-second toggle, we count 61 overflows ≈ 999 ms ≈ 1 second.

TCCR0B — Timer/Counter Control Register 0 B

The timer starts when you write the prescaler bits into TCCR0B:

  • CS02:CS01:CS00 = 1:0:1 → prescaler ÷1024, starts the timer immediately

Writing all CS bits to 0 stops the timer. WGM02 in TCCR0B (bit 3) is part of the waveform generation mode — leave at 0 for Normal Mode.

TIMSK0 — Timer Interrupt Mask Register 0

Setting bit TOIE0 (Timer Overflow Interrupt Enable, bit 0) in TIMSK0 enables the Timer0 Overflow Interrupt. When TCNT0 overflows, if TOIE0=1 and global interrupts are enabled, the CPU jumps to ISR(TIMER0_OVF_vect).

The Overflow ISR

The ISR increments a static (persistent across calls) overflow counter. Since every overflow is ≈ 16.38 ms, after 61 overflows ≈ 1000 ms, toggle the LED and reset the counter. The main loop stays empty — the timer handles everything in the background.

Timer0 vs Timer1 vs Timer2

  • Timer0 (8-bit): Used here. Also controls Arduino's millis()/delay() functions.
  • Timer1 (16-bit): Higher precision timing, servo control, input capture. See Exp 6.
  • Timer2 (8-bit, async): Can use external 32.768 kHz crystal for RTC functionality.

pretest.question: Which register controls the prescaler for Timer0?
pretest.explanation: TCCR0B (Timer/Counter 0 Control Register B) holds the CS0x (Clock Select) bits that select the prescaler and start/stop the timer.

pretest.question: Timer0 is an 8-bit timer. At what count value does it overflow in Normal Mode?
pretest.explanation: An 8-bit counter holds values 0–255. After reaching 255, the next increment overflows back to 0 and sets the TOV0 flag.

pretest.question: At 16 MHz with prescaler ÷1024, what is the approximate Timer0 overflow period?
pretest.explanation: Timer tick = 16MHz/1024 = 15625 Hz. Period per tick = 64 µs. 256 ticks × 64 µs = 16.384 ms per overflow.

pretest.question: Which register bit enables the Timer0 Overflow Interrupt?
pretest.explanation: TOIE0 (Timer Overflow Interrupt Enable, bit 0) in TIMSK0 enables the Timer0 overflow interrupt. When set and sei() active, overflow triggers the ISR.

pretest.question: What is the name of the Timer0 overflow ISR vector?
pretest.explanation: TIMER0_OVF_vect is the overflow interrupt vector for Timer0. TIMER0_COMPA_vect is for Compare Match A (CTC/PWM modes).

pretest.question: What does 'static' mean when used for a local variable inside an ISR?
options: Preserved between ISR calls — retains its value across invocations
pretest.explanation: A 'static' local variable is allocated in SRAM (like a global) but scoped to the function. It keeps its value between function calls, perfect for counting overflows.

pretest.question: To achieve a 1-second LED toggle with ÷1024 prescaler: how many overflows at 16.384 ms each are needed?
pretest.explanation: 1000 ms / 16.384 ms ≈ 61 overflows. After 61 overflows, ≈ 999 ms has elapsed — close enough to 1 second for visual timing.

pretest.question: What is the purpose of sei() in timer-based code?
options: Globally enables interrupts so the timer overflow ISR can fire
pretest.explanation: sei() sets the I-bit in SREG. Without this, even a correctly configured TIMSK0 and TCCR0B cannot trigger the ISR.

pretest.question: Which CS0x bit pattern sets prescaler to ÷1024?
pretest.explanation: Per the ATmega328P datasheet Table 14-9: CS02=1, CS01=0, CS00=1 selects clk_IO/1024. This is the setting for minimal power and longer overflow periods.

pretest.question: Why is it better to count overflows than to use _delay_ms() for 1-second timing?
options: The CPU is free to execute other code between overflows
pretest.explanation: _delay_ms(1000) blocks the CPU for 1 full second. With timer interrupts, the CPU only executes a few instructions per overflow (~60 per second), leaving it free between those ISR calls.

procedure: Include headers: #include <avr/io.h> and #include <avr/interrupt.h>. Define #define LED_PIN PB5. Do NOT include <util/delay.h> — no software delays are used in this experiment.
Configure the LED pin as output: DDRB |= (1 << LED_PIN);. Leave TCNT0 at its reset value of 0 — the timer will start counting from 0.

Set the Timer0 prescaler to ÷1024 by configuring the CS bits in TCCR0B. This simultaneously selects Normal Mode (WGM02=0 by default) and starts the timer: TCCR0B |= (1 << CS02) | (1 << CS00);. The timer is now running.
Enable the Timer0 Overflow Interrupt by setting the TOIE0 bit in TIMSK0: TIMSK0 |= (1 << TOIE0);. Without this, overflows are silent — the CPU never knows they occurred.
Enable global interrupts: sei();. The system is now fully armed. TCNT0 will overflow approximately every 16.384 ms and automatically invoke the ISR each time.
Leave the main loop completely empty: while(1) {}. The CPU simply spins here, immediately interrupted every 16.384 ms by the timer overflow. All work is in the background ISR.

Write the Timer0 Overflow ISR outside any function: use a static uint8_t overflowCount = 0; counter. Increment it on each overflow. When it reaches 61, toggle the LED using PORTB XOR: PORTB ^= (1 << LED_PIN); and reset the counter to 0.

Compile and flash. Observe the LED blinking at approximately 1 Hz (once per second) with zero software delay and a completely empty main loop. The ATmega328P's hardware timer handles all timing autonomously.

posttest.question: With the main while(1) loop empty, what is the CPU doing between overflows?
options: Executing Flash code — it loops in while(1) until each interrupt fires
posttest.explanation: An empty while(1) still executes — the CPU loops on a single 'RJMP' instruction back to itself, burning cycles. When an interrupt fires, it briefly jumps to the ISR, then returns.

posttest.question: How would you increase the LED toggle period from 1 second to 2 seconds without changing the prescaler?
options: Change the overflow count threshold from 61 to 122
posttest.explanation: Doubling the overflow count threshold (61 → 122) means the LED toggles after 122 × 16.384 ms ≈ 2 seconds.

posttest.question: Which prescaler setting gives Timer0 the longest overflow period?
posttest.explanation: ÷1024 is the maximum prescaler for Timer0, giving a tick every 64 µs at 16 MHz and an overflow every 16.384 ms — the longest period.

posttest.question: What is the TCNT0 register?
options: The actual 8-bit counter value that increments with each timer tick
posttest.explanation: TCNT0 (Timer/Counter 0) holds the current 8-bit count. You can read it to get elapsed time, or write to it to set a starting offset.

posttest.question: Why is Timer0 sometimes avoided in Arduino/AVR code that uses millis()?
options: Arduino's millis() uses Timer0 — reconfiguring it breaks millis() counting
posttest.explanation: The Arduino runtime uses Timer0 with a ÷64 prescaler to implement millis() and delay(). Changing TCCR0B breaks these built-in functions.

posttest.question: What does the SREG register contain?
options: CPU status flags including Carry, Zero, Overflow, and the I-bit
posttest.explanation: SREG (Status Register) holds 8 processor flags: I (global interrupt enable), T, H, S, V (overflow), N, Z (zero), C (carry).

posttest.question: In an ISR, interrupts are automatically:
posttest.explanation: Entering any AVR ISR clears the I-bit in SREG. RETI re-enables them. This prevents the overflow ISR from being interrupted by another overflow.

posttest.question: What is a watchdog timer used for?
posttest.explanation: The WDT has an independent oscillator. If firmware fails to 'pet' it within its timeout window, it forces a system reset — essential for reliable embedded products.

posttest.question: Which is NOT a valid ATmega328P port?
posttest.explanation: ATmega328P has only Port B, C, and D. No Port A exists on this chip (unlike larger AVR devices).

posttest.question: What happens to SRAM when power is removed?
posttest.explanation: SRAM is volatile memory. All variable state is instantly lost on power-off or reset.

feedback: Brilliant! You've broken free from blocking delays by harnessing hardware-autonomous timers with interrupt-driven callbacks. This is the foundation of all real-time embedded systems — timers running independently while the CPU handles complex tasks.
